factSheet.title: CNH vs John Deere
factSheet.intro: Latest public results verified October 10, 2026. Start with the takeaway, then read the detailed numbers and the reasons behind them. All dollar amounts are USD; quarterly results are global.

industries.title: Agriculture
industries.description: CNH Agriculture overlaps with two John Deere segments. Small Agriculture & Turf also includes turf products.

peers.name: John Deere
peers.focus: Production & Precision Agriculture; Small Agriculture & Turf

industries.title: Construction
industries.description: CNH Construction overlaps with Deere Construction & Forestry, which also includes forestry and roadbuilding.

headcount.definition: Worldwide employees at year-end; all company businesses.
Worldwide employees at fiscal year-end; all company businesses.

operating.scopeNote: CNH non-GAAP measure. Excludes Financial Services and Construction.
One of two agriculture segments. Deere’s quarter ends later; segment exclusions differ from CNH.

Global Construction business; CNH non-GAAP measure.

grossMargins.note: Reported. $747m gross profit / $4,143m net sales. Agriculture + Construction; excludes Financial Services.
Calculated: ($10,999m net sales − $7,950m matching equipment COGS) / $10,999m. Includes agriculture, turf, construction, and forestry; excludes Financial Services.

stock.note: CNH and Deere trade on NYSE in USD. Fixed regular-session closing-price snapshot; dividends are excluded. Compare matching-date percentage returns, not dollar share prices.

methodology: Latest available quarters: CNH Q2 ended June 30, 2026; Deere fiscal Q3 ended August 2, 2026. They overlap but are not the same calendar period. Each year-over-year change uses the same company’s prior-year quarter.

Equipment scopes differ: CNH Industrial Activities includes Agriculture and Construction; Deere Equipment Operations also includes turf and forestry. Gross profit uses the matching equipment net sales and cost of sales.

CNH adjusted EBIT is non-GAAP. Deere segment operating profit excludes corporate expenses and certain financing and other items. Summed Deere segment profit is calculated, not company net income or a normalized CNH EBIT measure.

Company net-income comparisons use income attributable to the parent in both columns. CNH’s separately reported consolidated net income is $141m versus $217m; the attributable amounts shown here are $138m versus $213m.

Deere Q3 2026 included $110m tariff recoveries; Q3 2025 included $61m equipment impairment expense. CNH Q2 2026 included $27m restructuring and transformation expense versus $5m in Q2 2025. Reported profit changes include these effects.

Headcounts are annual global employee totals at the stated dates, not current North America staffing or comparable average FTEs. Stock returns use matching dates and exclude dividends. Neither establishes workforce productivity or the cause of a share-price move.

refresh.note: A new edition is scheduled for the first day of each month at 9 a.m. America/New_York. Only verified public data is published; source periods remain visible. Saved rounds retain their original facts and questions.

comparison.periodNote: Latest available quarters, with different end dates: CNH June 30; John Deere August 2. Changes compare each company with its own prior-year quarter. These are global results.

highlights.title: Sales grew at both companies
highlights.meaning: Both sold more in dollar terms than a year earlier. Sales growth alone does not show how much profit remained.
highlights.why: Pricing, currency and product mix can lift sales even when unit demand stays weak. Read margins alongside revenue.

highlights.title: CNH kept less of each sales dollar
highlights.figures: Equipment gross margin: CNH 18.0% · John Deere 27.72%
highlights.meaning: For every $100 of equipment sales, about $18 remained at CNH after product costs, versus $27.72 at Deere, before other business expenses.
highlights.why: A thinner margin leaves less room to fund development, overhead and future investment. Different products and quarter dates affect this comparison.

highlights.title: Our profit trend was weaker
highlights.figures: Parent net income: CNH −35.2% · John Deere +7.0%
highlights.meaning: CNH’s attributable profit fell to $138m; Deere’s rose to $1,379m. Deere’s large-ag segment still had lower sales and profit.
highlights.why: Focus on what we can improve: quality, cost and execution, while planning capacity around demand. Deere’s other businesses helped its overall result.

metrics.label: Total company revenue
metrics.meaning: Money earned from equipment, financing and other activities before expenses. Deere’s larger total shows company scale.
metrics.why: Revenue growth can come from price, currency or mix as well as units sold. It is not a market-share calculation.

metrics.label: Equipment net sales
metrics.meaning: Equipment revenue excludes Financial Services. CNH grew 3.0%; Deere grew 6.2% from the rounded figures.
metrics.why: Comparing growth with the same prior-year quarter gives context for demand and execution. Product coverage still differs.

metrics.label: Equipment cost of sales
metrics.meaning: The product costs associated with equipment sales. CNH’s costs rose faster than its sales.
metrics.why: When product costs consume more of each sales dollar, gross margin falls. This is not total company spending.
metrics.scopeNote: Deere uses equipment cost of sales, not consolidated cost of sales ($7,939m).

metrics.label: Equipment gross profit

deere.scope: Calculated: net sales − equipment cost of sales

metrics.meaning: Revenue remaining after product costs: CNH fell $82m; Deere rose $270m.
metrics.why: This pool must still fund overhead, development, financing costs and taxes. It is not net income.

metrics.label: Equipment gross margin
metrics.meaning: CNH fell 2.6 percentage points while Deere improved about 0.89 points. The current reported gap is 9.72 points.
metrics.why: Margin translates different company sizes into dollars retained per $100 of sales. It still reflects business mix and accounting scope.

metrics.label: Equipment operating profit

deere.scope: Calculated sum of three segment operating profits

metrics.meaning: CNH’s adjusted equipment profit fell $57m. Deere’s three equipment segments together rose $283m.
metrics.why: This helps locate the operating-profit trend before financing and tax; the measures have different exclusions.
metrics.scopeNote: CNH includes unallocated/elimination items of −$18m (prior −$74m). Deere sums 527 + 622 + 436 = 1,585 (prior 580 + 485 + 237 = 1,302) and excludes corporate expenses. Different exclusions prevent a normalized EBIT comparison.

metrics.label: Equipment operating margin

deere.scope: Calculated sum of segment profit ÷ equipment net sales

metrics.meaning: CNH retained about $4 per $100 at this stage; Deere’s segment measure retained about $14.41.
metrics.why: Read the segment detail to see where profits improved or weakened. The gap cannot be assigned directly to staffing or efficiency.
metrics.scopeNote: Deere: 1,585 ÷ 10,999 × 100 = 14.41%; prior 1,302 ÷ 10,357 = 12.57%. Company-specific profit definitions differ.

metrics.label: Net income attributable to the parent

cnh.scope: CNH Industrial N.V. attributable net income

metrics.meaning: Profit for the parent’s shareholders after expenses and taxes. CNH fell 35.2%; Deere rose 7.0%.
metrics.why: This is the company-wide earnings outcome. It includes Financial Services and items outside factory performance.
metrics.scopeNote: CNH’s headline consolidated net income ($141m) includes $3m attributable to noncontrolling interests.

metrics.label: Diluted earnings per share
metrics.meaning: Earnings divided by diluted share count. Read each company’s year-over-year movement.
metrics.why: The dollar EPS level is affected by share count; a higher EPS alone does not establish a better business or investment.

metrics.label: Financial Services net income
metrics.meaning: CNH financing profit fell $16m; Deere financing profit rose $14m.
metrics.why: Financing is a separate earnings engine from making equipment. Do not mix this net-income figure with equipment operating profit.

drivers.title: Agriculture: where the gap comes from

rows.meaning: Nearly flat sales produced $93m less profit. The margin fell 2.9 percentage points.
rows.why: CNH cites lower South America volumes, unfavorable North America/EMEA mix, tariffs, higher SG&A/R&D and lower joint-venture results.

rows.meaning: Large-ag sales and profit declined, but its reported margin was 8.0 points above CNH Agriculture.
rows.why: Deere cites lower shipments and higher production costs, partly offset by pricing and currency.

rows.meaning: This separate business grew sales and profit and helped lift Deere’s overall result.
rows.why: Deere cites higher shipments and favorable mix/pricing, partly offset by higher production costs.

drivers.takeaway: Interpretation: Deere’s agriculture businesses were not moving in the same direction. Combining them into one headline would hide the large-ag decline.
drivers.scopeNote: CNH has one Agriculture segment; Deere has two, including turf. Its segment operating profit and CNH adjusted EBIT have different exclusions. Periods also differ.

drivers.title: Construction: more sales did not mean more CNH profit

rows.meaning: Sales grew 12.0%, but profit fell $20m and margin fell 2.8 points.
rows.why: CNH cites tariffs and higher R&D, partly offset by more volume and lower SG&A. Sales included shipments delayed from Q1.

rows.meaning: Sales and profit both grew. The reported margin was 10.4 points above CNH Construction.
rows.why: Deere cites higher volume and pricing for sales; favorable pricing drove profit growth, partly offset by higher SG&A/R&D.

drivers.takeaway: Interpretation: CNH sold more while earning less. The immediate question is how pricing and execution can cover product and development costs.
drivers.scopeNote: Deere also includes forestry and roadbuilding. Reported margins are directional context, not a like-for-like staffing or efficiency target.

stockMeaning.meaning: CNH trailed John Deere over all three shown windows. One-month returns were −18.06% and −8.31%; CNH lagged by 9.75 percentage points. Over one year both rose, with Deere rising more.
stockMeaning.why: Prices reflect investor expectations as well as results. These closes establish the return gap; they do not establish its cause or measure plant performance.

questions.prompt: CNH equipment sales grew 3.03%; parent net income fell 35.21%. What does this tell us?
options: Sales growth alone does not guarantee profit growth.
More revenue always creates more profit.
The sales figure includes only financing income.
Net income is the same as gross profit.
questions.explanation: CNH equipment sales rose from $4,021m to $4,143m, while attributable net income fell from $213m to $138m. Revenue is before expenses; net income is after them. Read the cost and margin changes to explain the result.
questions.discussion: Which costs, pricing and product-mix changes matter most for our decisions?
